**Sūrat al-Ma'ārij**

It is also called Sūrat al-Mawāqi' and Sūrat Sa'ala. It is Makki (revealed in Mecca) by consensus, as al-Qurtubi said. In *Majma' al-Bayan*, it is reported from al-Hasan that the exception is His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 24]. Its verses number forty-three according to the Syrian count and forty-two according to others. It is like a continuation of Sūrat al-Haqqah, covering the rest of the description of the Resurrection and the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas said that it was revealed immediately after Sūrat al-Haqqah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿A petitioner petitioned for a punishment that will surely befall﴾. That is, one who calls upon it has called for it. So *al-su'al* (asking) here carries the meaning of *al-du'a'* (supplication), and for this reason it takes *bi* (with), as the verb takes it in His saying: ﴿calling therein for every kind of fruit﴾ [al-Dukhan: 55]. The intended meaning is seeking the punishment and demanding it, and this has nothing to do with *tadmin* (the imbuing of one verb with the meaning of another). It has been said that the verb is imbued with the meaning of *al-ihtimam* (concern) and *al-i'tina'* (attentiveness), or that it is a *majaz* (metaphor) for that, which is why it takes *bi*. It has also been said that the *ba'* is superfluous, and that it has the meaning of *'an* (about), as in His saying: ﴿then ask about Him one who is well-informed﴾ [al-Furqan: 59]. The petitioner is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, as al-Nasa'i and a group related, and al-Hakim authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

This was also narrated from Ibn Juraij, al-Suddi and the majority, who said, in denial and mockery: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. It has been said that he was Abu Jahl, who said: ﴿so cause fragments of the sky to fall upon us﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 187].

It has also been said that he was al-Harith ibn al-Nu'man al-Fihri, and the reason was that when the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, reached him: "Whoever I am his master, 'Ali is his master," he said: "O Allah, if what Muhammad ﷺ says is true, then rain down upon us stones from the sky." He had not stayed long before Allah struck him with a stone that landed on his brain and came out from his lower parts, and he died on the spot.

You know that this statement of his, peace be upon him, about the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, was made at Ghadir Khumm, and that was in the final years of the Hijrah. Therefore, what was revealed about it cannot be Makki according to the well-known view regarding its interpretation. You have heard what has been said about the Makki status of this sūrah. It has also been said that the one meant is the Messenger ﷺ, who hastened their punishment. It has also been said that he is Nuh, peace be upon him, who asked for the punishment of his people.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *sāla* with an *alif*, like *qāla sā'il* with a *yā'* after the *alif*. It has been said that it is permissible that the *hamzah* of the verb was replaced with an *alif*, and this substitution (*ibdal*) is irregular; the regular analogy for this is *bayna bayna* (an intermediate articulation between *hamzah* and the vowel). It is also permissible that it follows the dialect of those who say *salat* → *asāl*, which Sibawayh transmitted. In *al-Kashshaf*, it is from *al-su'al* (the hamzated root), that is, in meaning and not as a derivation, as shown by *wa-humā yatasā'alān* (and they two ask one another). This indicates that it is a hollow verb, which comes, and it is not from easing the *hamzah* at all. It has also been said that *al-su'al* is with the pure *waw*, with *ḍamm* and *kasr* on the *sīn*. His saying *yatasāyalān* should be *yatasāwalān*, so that its *alif* is changed from a *waw*, as in *qāla* and *khāfa*. This is what Abu 'Ali chose in *al-Hujjah*, and he mentioned in it that Abu 'Uthman related from Abu Zayd that he heard from the Arabs one who says *humā yatasāwalān*. Then, in the claim that *salat* → *tusālu* is the dialect of Quraysh, there is some hesitation, and the apparent view is otherwise. They cited for the occurrence of *sāla* the verse of Hassan satirizing the tribe of Hudhayl, when they asked the Prophet ﷺ to permit them fornication:

*"The Hudhayl asked the Messenger of Allah for an abomination;*
*Hudhayl went astray in what they said, and was not right."*

And another's saying:

*"The two of them asked me for divorce when they saw me;*
*Say, what is wrong with me? You two have come to me with something objectionable."*

It is also permissible that *sāla* is from *al-saylān* (flowing). It is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, *sāla sayl* (a flood flowed). Ibn Jinni said: *al-sayl* here is the flowing water, and its origin is the verbal noun from your saying *sāla al-mā'u sayлan* (the water flowed), except that it was applied to the agent, as in His saying: ﴿if your water should become sunken﴾ [al-Mulk: 30], meaning *ghā'iran* (sunken). The expression has been loosely applied to the valley, so it is said that the meaning is: a valley flowed with a punishment that will surely befall. The use of the past tense is said to serve to affirm the certain occurrence of the punishment, either in this world, which is the punishment of the Day of Badr, when al-Nadr and Abu Jahl were killed that day, or in the Hereafter, which is the punishment of the Fire. It is reported from Zayd ibn Thabit that *sā'il* is the name of a valley in Hell. Ibn al-Mundhir and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibn 'Abbas what admits of this meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 2:

﴿For the disbelievers﴾ is another attribute (sifah) of "a punishment," meaning: one that is incumbent (kaa'inin) ﴿for the disbelievers﴾. Or it is a complement (silah) of "will befall" (waqi'), and the lam is for causation (ta'lil), or it carries the meaning of "upon" (ala). This is supported by the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): "upon the disbelievers." Even if what is reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah is sound, that the people of Makkah, when the Prophet (ﷺ) warned them of a punishment, asked about it: upon what it would descend and upon whom it would fall, and so it was revealed, then this would be the beginning of a speech answering the questioner, meaning: it is for the disbelievers.

And His, the Exalted's, words ﴿there is none to avert it﴾ are another attribute of "a punishment," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, to specify it by the attribute or by the action; or from the pronoun in ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ on the assumption that it is an attribute of "a punishment," according to what has been said; or it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf); or it is a sentence emphasizing the "it is" (huwa) in "for the disbelievers," as you have heard just now. So do not be heedless.

The Exalted One's saying ﴿from God﴾ is related to *dafi'* (repeller), and *min* is ibtida'iyyah (denoting origin, "from"). The meaning is that there is no repeller who can turn it back from His side, the Mighty and Majestic, because His will is attached to it, glory be to Him. It was also said that it is related to *waqi'* (befalling), and it was said that this is valid only according to other than the view of al-Hasan and Qatada. On this view, there is a separation by a foreign element, because ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ according to that is an answer to a question. Then, the attachment to *waqi'* according to views other than those two, if ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ is also taken as part of its complement, would be more apparent; otherwise, there would be a separation between the object and its governing word by something that is not part of its completion. However, it is not wholly foreign in every respect.

﴿Lord of the ascending stairways﴾: *al-ma'arij* is, in the language, the plural of *al-darajat* (degrees). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by them is the heavens, in which the angels ascend from one heaven to another. Some did not specify them, and said: that is, possessor of the ascents by which the angels ascend with the commands and prohibitions. It was also said: they are immaterial stations in which deeds and remembrances are located, or stages of the spiritual path, by which the believing wayfarers progress, or the ranks of the angels, upon them be peace.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada that it is to be interpreted as virtues and blessings, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi 'Abbas reported something similar. It was also said: they are the chambers which God, Exalted is He, has prepared for His friends in Paradise. But the most fitting interpretation, in light of what the context requires of awe-inspiring magnitude, is that which is more indicative of His might, Mighty and Majestic is He, and the greatness of His dominion, exalted is His state.

[p. 57]

"The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him." It is said that "the Spirit" means Gabriel (peace be upon him), as the majority of scholars hold. He is singled out for mention because of his distinction and excellence, on the basis of the well-known view that he (peace be upon him) is the most excellent of the angels. It is also said that he is singled out merely for honour, even though he (peace be upon him) is not the most excellent of them, on the basis of what has been said, that Israfil (peace be upon him) is more excellent than he.

Mujahid said: "the Spirit" refers to angels who guard the angels who guard the children of Adam. The guarding angels do not see them, just as we do not see our own guardian angels.

It is also said that they are a kind of creature who guard the angels in general, just as the angels guard people. It is said that they are an angel of great stature who stands alone on the Day of Resurrection in a rank, while all the angels stand in another rank. Abu Salih said: they are a creation in the form of humans, but they are not humans. Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: "the Spirit" is the spirit of the dead person at the moment his soul is taken, though he perhaps meant the believing dead person.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), al-Kisa'i, Ibn Miqsam, and Za'ida (from al-A'mash) read "yaʿruju" with the letter yāʾ (third-person masculine form). "To Him" (ilayhi): it is said this means to His Throne, the place from which it descends, or to His command, glory be to Him. It is also said that it is of the same type as the saying of Abraham (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], meaning: to where my Lord has commanded me.

It is also said that the meaning is "to the place of His righteousness and honour, exalted is He," with the speech being elliptical (an omitted noun). It is said that it means "to the place that is the ultimate destination," as the context indicates. It was explained as the place of the angels (peace be upon them) in the heaven. Most of the early generations (al-Salaf) count this among the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses whose meaning is not to be fixed by literal reading), while affirming the transcendence of the Mighty and Majestic One above place, corporeality, and the implications that do not befit the majesty of Divinity.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in a Day the extent of which is fifty thousand years﴾, meaning of your years. The apparent connection is with "ascend" (taʿruju). "Day" (al-yawm) here means a period of time, and what is meant is the duration in which people stand before the Lord of the worlds, until the people of Paradise settle in Paradise and the people of the Fire settle in the Fire, from the Last Day, which has no end.

Pointing to this is what Imam Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, and al-Bayhaqi in (his book) al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about a Day the extent of which is fifty thousand years: how long is this day? He (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand my soul is, it will be made light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than the obligatory prayer that he prays in this world.'"

There is disagreement about what is meant by this measurement according to this view. It is said that the indication is to the lengthening of that day because of its severity, not that it is literally this number. This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The Arabs describe times of hardship and sorrow as long, and times of ease and joy as short. Among this is the saying of the poet:

"From the shortness of the night when you visit me, I complain, and you complain of its length."

And his saying:

"My night and the night of Layla, their differences have prevented my sleep, with length, and length, O bliss, if only they were equal.
It bestows length upon my night whenever Layla is stingy with length, and if she bestows it, she is stingy."

And his saying:

"And a day which, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin for us and the clapping of the lutes."

And so on, to what is almost impossible to count.

In his (ﷺ) statement in the previous report: "It will be made light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer," there is an indication of this. Likewise is what is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar as his saying: "On that day, chairs of gold will be placed for the believers, the clouds will shade them, that day will be shortened for them, and it will be made easy, until it is like a day of your days in this world."

And it is for consideration, according to this view, what is the wisdom in specifying the number mentioned. It is also said that it is on its literal and real meaning, and that in that day there are fifty stations, each station being a thousand years of the years of this world, literally. It is also said that the fifty are literal, except that the meaning is the amount of time in which the judgment is decided with justice, equal to what would be decided in fifty thousand years of the days of this world. This was reported from ʿIkrima.

Some of them pointed out that the measurement mentioned is, according to this view, a metaphor for what it entails of the great number of reckonings that take place in it, or a kinaya (figurative expression), as if it were said: "in a day in which the reckoning is abundant and so long that, if it were conducted by the swiftest of reckoners, while in this world, it would take fifty thousand years." The specification of the ascent of the angels and the Spirit to that day, even though their ascent is realized at other times too, is to indicate the greatness of its terror, the people's cutting off from everything but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and their awaiting His command, glory be to Him, concerning them. Or it is to indicate the greatness of the terror in another way. Whatever the case, the sentence is a resumptive (istinaf) emphatic statement for what the speech was brought to convey.

It is said that the phrase is connected to "waqiʿ" (befalling, from the verse ﴿a punishment that will befall﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 1]); it is said it is connected to "dafiʿ" (repelling, from the verse ﴿none can repel it﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 2]); and it is said it is connected to "sal" (flowing), if it is derived from the flowing (sayalan), not from asking (suʾal), because it (the punishment) has not yet occurred in it. The meaning of "the Day" according to these views is the same as what was meant earlier in (the verse) ﴿and the angels and the Spirit ascend﴾ to Him, and it is a digression when describing Him, the Mighty and Majestic, as "the Lord of the ascending stairways" (dhi al-maʿarij). It is also said that it is connected to "taʿruju," as is apparent, except that the ascent is in this world, and the meaning is: the angels and the Spirit ascend to His Throne, exalted is He, and they cover, in a day of your days, what a human would cover in fifty thousand years if his journey in it were assumed.

It was reported from Ibn Ishaq, Mundhir ibn Sa'id, Mujahid, and a group, and it is also a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, that there is disagreement about determining the distance. It is said that it is from the surface of the earth to the farthest point of the Throne. It is said that it is from the bottom of the lowest seventh earth to the Throne, and it has been detailed that:

[p. 58]

the thickness of each earth is five hundred years, the distance between each earth and the next is five hundred years, the distance between the highest earth and the lowest heaven is five hundred years, the thickness of each heaven is likewise five hundred years, the distance between each two heavens is likewise five hundred years, and the distance between the highest heaven and the concave base of the Kursi (Footstool) is likewise five hundred years. The total of these is fourteen thousand years, and from the concave base of the Kursi to the Throne is a journey of thirty-six thousand years, so the total is fifty thousand years.

There is a report that Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas similar to this, but it probably is not authentic. Yet this speed is not far-fetched from the angels (peace be upon them) according to whoever has considered the speed of the movement of light and knows that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is capable of all things.

Some people considered this duration, from the earth to the Throne, as both ascent and descent, and considered it likewise from the earth to the concave surface of the lowest heaven, in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day the extent of which is a thousand years﴾ [al-Sajda: 5]. Whoever takes either of these two matters will consider here the convex surface of the lowest heaven and the earth. The Sufis' views on this will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.

It is also said that the statement is an explanation of the extreme height of those ascending stairways and the distance of their reach, by way of illustration and imagination. What is meant is that they are at the extreme of distance and elevation, in a figurative sense according to some aspects of the "stairways," or in a physical sense as in others.

The meaning is not to define (the measurement). It was reported from ʿIkrima that this duration is the duration of this world from the time it was created until the Hour is established, and that no one knows how much of it has passed and how much remains. That is, the angels ascend to Him during the duration of this world and the continuation of this structure. This requires authentic transmission. The apparent meaning is that by "this world" he meant what is opposed to the Hereafter, and it includes the Throne and the like. This is refuted by what was reported from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, in answer to one who asked him when Allah created the Throne, which contradicts it, for it indicates that what has passed from the first time of its creation until today exceeds fifty thousand years by thousands upon thousands of years, which none can count except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And this is perhaps more worthy of acceptance than what ʿIkrima said.

The truth is that no one knows the beginning of creation or the duration of the continuation of this structure except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Nevertheless, we know, by the grace of Allah the Exalted, that this world is created with a temporal origination (hudūth zamānī), and that the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens (likewise), and that creation will come forth before Allah the Exalted, the One, the Subduer.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 5:

﴿So be patient with patience that is beautiful.﴾ This is consequent upon His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿A questioner asked﴾, and is connected to it in meaning, because the questioning was [done] with mockery, obstinacy and denial, on the basis that the questioner was al-Nadr and his like, and that is something which would vex him, upon him be blessings and peace. Or [the questioning] was out of impatience and urging for the victory, on the basis that he (ﷺ) was himself the questioner, so it is as if it were said: "Be patient and do not hasten, for what has been promised will certainly occur." The meaning on this [view] is also [the same] according to the reading of the one who reads "sāla sā'ilun" (from al-sayalān, flowing), like the reading "sāla saylun" (a torrent flowed), and its being consequent upon "sa'ala" (asked, from al-su'āl) does not appear if the questioner was Nuh, upon him be peace. And the beautiful patience, as related by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul from Ibn Abbas, is that there be no complaint in it to anyone other than Allah, Exalted is He. And it is related from Abd al-A'la ibn al-Hajjaj that it is [patience] in which the person afflicted by the calamity is among the people in such a way that it is not known who he is.

﴿They see it﴾, i.e., the punishment that is to befall them, or the day mentioned in His words ﴿on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾, and so on. This is on the basis that the intended day is the Day of Reckoning, and that it is connected (*mutaʿalliq*, the grammatical element it depends on) to ﴿ascends﴾ (تَعْرُجُ), as you heard earlier, or to ﴿repelling﴾ (دافِع), or to ﴿befalling﴾ (واقِع), or to ﴿flowing﴾ (سال, from السَّيَلان), or that it is the Day of Resurrection, indicated by ﴿befalling﴾ (واقِع) in a particular way. As for what the *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary) implies by restricting the return of the pronoun to the Day of Resurrection to the case where ﴿on a Day﴾ is connected to ﴿befalling﴾ within it, there is scrutiny in it, and in meaning.

﴿They see it﴾ means they believe it (يَعْتَقِدُونَهُ). ﴿Distant﴾ (بَعِيدًا) means distant from possibility, and the intended sense is that they believe it to be impossible; or distant from occurrence, and the intended sense is that they believe it will not occur at all, even though it is possible in its essence. The statements of the disbelievers of Mecca concerning the Day of Resurrection and the Reckoning are open to both meanings. Indeed, you may hear them speaking in a way that nearly suggests its occurrence, when they claim that their gods will intercede for them. So they vacillate about it, like the chameleon (ḥirbāʾ) changing its colour.

If the punishment is taken to mean the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, then it is, for them, like the Day of Resurrection. Or it is that it does not befall them at all, since they claim that their gods will repel it from them. If, however, the punishment is taken to mean the punishment of this world, then the apparent meaning is that they do not deny its possibility, but only deny its occurrence. The claim that they deny its essential possibility can hardly be sustained.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 7:

﴿And We see it as near.﴾ That is: near in terms of possibility. The use of this expression (the verb "We see") is for the sake of harmonizing with what is said before it (mushakalah), as has been said, since [the verse] says "﴿They see it as far﴾" and "We see it as near," [the verb] "see" being used in both. For the possible is [already] possible, and there is no sense in describing the possible as "near to possibility," since it is included within its scope. What is meant is describing it with possibility, i.e. "and We see it as possible." This is according to the first interpretation of "﴿They see it as far﴾," [meaning far in possibility]. Or [the phrase means] "We see it as near" to occurring, and this is according to the second interpretation of it. It may be said that the same applies to the first interpretation as well, in the sense that they "﴿see it as far﴾" from possibility while We see it as near to occurrence, let alone possibility. This is perhaps better than supposing possibility in both clauses.

The clause "﴿Indeed they﴾" and so on is a reason (ta'lil) for the command to be patient. It has also been said that if the one being hasty is an-Nadr and his like, then the clause is resumed (mustaʼnafah), explaining the doubt behind their mockery and answering it. If the one being hasty is the Prophet (ﷺ), then it is a reason for what the command to be patient implies of abandoning haste, namely that Our seeing that [event] as near makes one confident and leads to abandoning haste.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 8:

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿On the day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾, may be connected to "close" (qarīban), or to a implied verb indicated by "will fall" (wāqi'), which means "it will fall," or it may be a substitute (badal) for "on a day" (fī yawmin), if the latter is taken as governed by it and not by "ascend" (ta'rujս). The accusative case is considered in view of the fact that the place (maḥall) of the prepositional phrase is that, since it is not a substitute for the genitive alone. Thus Abu Hayyan's stipulation that the preposition be superfluous (zā'id), or like it, such as rubba, in order to observe the place, is not correct. The substitution does not need the commitment that the vowel of "yawma" is a built (binā'iyya) vowel, according to the view of the Kufans who permit this, even though it is attached to an inflected noun. It has been mentioned that on these three estimations, the intended punishment is the punishment of the Resurrection. As for if the punishment of this world is intended, it is necessary that the estimation be: "On the day the sky will be such-and-such, such-and-such will happen." It seems that when they asked for the punishment hastily, they were answered that it is near in occurrence. Then it was said: let that be easy in comparison with what has been prepared for you, ﴿On the day the sky will be like molten brass﴾. Then the punishment which is the punishment (al-'adhāb alladhī huwa al-'adhāb) occurs. Then it is not hidden that the beginning (al-bidāya) is possible on the estimation that "on a day" is connected to "ascend" as well, based on the view that the intended meaning of it is also the Day of Resurrection, as we have previously mentioned, and that the preferable [option], when it is connected to "close," is that the nearness is not taken as possibility in the sense of inherent possibility, because restricting it to the day contains a kind of ambiguity.

And if the pronouns in ﴿they see it﴾ and ﴿We see it﴾ refer to the Day of Resurrection, it entails the occurrence of time within time in our saying: the Day of Resurrection occurs on the day when it is like molten brass. This is answered by what is not hidden. Al-Bahr permitted that it be a substitute for the pronoun in "We see it," if it refers to the Day of Resurrection. In al-Irshad, it is said that it is connected to "is not," which has no hindrance. Some [said] it is an object (maf'ūl bihi) of a deleted verb, and its connection to "We see it," as Makki said, is not valid; likewise its connection to "they will be made to see them," as he related. Similar to this is what might be said: its connection to "will wish" (yawaddu), which comes after, so reflect. As for al-Muhl: Ahmad, al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the dregs of oil, which is what is at its bottom.

Others said: al-Muhl is what has been melted over a flame (muhl) from metals, and the intended meaning is that the sky will be fragile (wāhiya). 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatada regarding the verse that the sky now is green, and that it will be transformed on the Day of Resurrection into another color, to redness.

﴿And the mountains will be like wool﴾ — like tufts of wool, without qualification. Others said: "red," or "dyed in various colors." A group preferred the last view, because the mountains differ in color: some have white and red streaks, and some are jet-black (gharabib sud). When they are carded and scattered in the air, they resemble ʿihn, that is, carded wool, as in the verse of al-Qari'ah: ﴿when the mountains are like carded wool﴾, when the wind has scattered it. And from al-Hasan: the mountains will move with the winds, then they will crumble, then they will become like ʿihn, then they will be blown away and become scattered dust (habaʾ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 10:

﴿And no close friend will ask a close friend,﴾ that is, no close relative, who is concerned for a close relative, asks him about his condition, nor speaks to him, because each of them is being tested by what preoccupies him from that. Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd ibn Humayd related it from Qatadah. In another narration from him: he does not ask him about his condition, because it is evident. It was also said: he does not ask him to bear any of his burdens for him, because of his despair of that. It was also said: he does not ask him for intercession. In al-Bahr: he does not ask him for his help or his benefit, because he knows that he will not find that with him. Perhaps the first is more emphatic in conveying the terror. **﴿Nay﴾** is a rebuke to the criminal against wishing to be ransomed, and an explicit statement that rescue is impossible. The pronoun in **﴿Indeed it﴾** refers to the Fire, which is implied by the mention of the punishment. His saying, exalted is He, **﴿Blazing fire (Laza)﴾**, is the predicate of *inna* (the particle of emphasis). *Laza* is a proper name for Hellfire, or for the second of its levels (*darakat*), and it is transferred (*manqul*) from *al-laza* (pure flame, blazing fire). It is not declined (*man' al-sarf*) because of its status as a proper name (*'alamiyya*) and its feminine form (*ta'nith*). It was also permitted that it means "flame" as an intensification, as if all of it were pure flame. The omission of the nunation (*tanwin*) is either to treat pausing (*wasl*) as stopping (*waqf*), or because it is a generic proper name (*'alam jins*) that has been diverted (*mu'addal*) from what contains the definite article *al-*, as in *sihr* when you mean a specific instance of magic.

His saying, exalted is He, **﴿Stripping away the extremities (nazzaʿa lil-shawa)﴾**, means the limbs, such as the hand and the foot, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Humayd from Mujahid and Abu Salih, and as said by al-Raghib and others. It has also been said that it means the parts of the body that are not vital, which is why it is said "he shot and wounded (*ashwa*)" when he did not kill. Or it is the plural of *shawa*, which is the skin of the head. They recited the verse of al-A'sha:

*Qatila said: "What has happened to him, that his scalp has been covered with white hair?"*

This was reported from Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Qurra ibn Khalid and Ibn Jubayr. Ibn Abi Shaybah reported it from Mujahid, and he also reported from Abu Salih and al-Suddi the explanation of it as the flesh of the two shins. From Ibn Jubayr, it is the sinew and the heel. From Abu al-Aliyah, it is the fine features of the face. He explained its "stripping" in this sense as its devouring of him, so it devours him and then returns, and so on. It is in the accusative by an implied verb (*bi-taqdir*), meaning "I mean" or "I specify". This is what is meant by those who said it is in the accusative by specification (*ikhtisas*) for the sake of terrifying. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and the governing element of it is **﴿Blazing fire﴾**, even though it is a proper name, because of what it contains of the meaning of blazing (*talazzi*), just as a proper name governs an adverb of time in his saying: "I am Abu al-Minhal, at times (*ba'da al-ahyan*)", meaning "I am well known at times." This is what Abu Hayyan said, and the discourse of *al-Kashshaf* points to it.

Al-Khafaji said: **﴿Blazing fire﴾** means "blazing (*mutalazziyya*)", and the circumstantial accusative is from the hidden pronoun within it, not from "it" in the earlier sense, because it is indefinite, or a predicate. In the coming of a circumstantial accusative from something like this there is what there is. It was also said that it is an emphatic circumstantial accusative, as in his saying:

*I am the son of Dara, known by it as my lineage. And is there any shame in Dara, O people?*

The governing element is either *ahaquhu* (I have the right to it), or the predicate, because it implies the meaning of "named", or the subject (*mubtada'*), because it contains the meaning of an alert (*tanbih*) or the meaning of a sentence. This is the view that al-Radi approved. It was also said that it is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun of **﴿calls﴾**, placed before it. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the pronoun of **﴿Indeed it﴾** be ambiguous (*mubham*), explained by the predicate, which is **﴿Blazing fire﴾**. This was discussed with what the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqun*) rejected.

Most readers recited **﴿stripping away﴾** with the nominative (*nazzaʿatun*), on the basis that it is a second predicate of *inna*, or an attribute (*sifa*) of *Laza*. This is clear if we consider it indefinite, and likewise if we consider it a generic proper name, because it is like the definite with the article of the genus (*lam al-jins*) in being treated as an indefinite. It was permitted in this reading that the pronoun of **﴿Indeed it﴾** refers to the matter (*al-qissa*), and **﴿Laza﴾** is the subject (*mubtada'*), on the basis that it is definite, and **﴿stripping away﴾** is its predicate.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 70, verses 19–20:**

﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious (halu')﴾. Al-Hala' (anxiety, impatience) is the quickness of distress when harm touches a person, and the quickness of withholding when good touches him. This comes from their saying "a she-camel that is halu'," meaning one quick in its pace.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and others narrated from Ikrimah, who said: Ibn Abbas was asked about the halu', and he said: "It is as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When harm touches him﴾, and so on." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan that he was asked about this as well, and he recited the verse. Something similar is related from Tha'lab, who said: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Tahir said to me, "What is al-hala'?" I said: "Allah the Exalted has already explained it, and there can be no explanation clearer than His explanation, glory be to Him, meaning His saying the Exalted: ﴿When harm touches him﴾, and so on." A parallel to this is the verse of the poet:

*"The discerning one who thinks of you the thought,*
*as if he had seen and heard."*

The emphatic clause is in the place of a justification for what precedes it. As for ﴿al-insan﴾ (the human being), there are two views, whether it refers to the species or to the disbeliever. The second has been supported by what al-Tastiyy narrated from Ibn Abbas, that the verse was about Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. Yet the intention of the species does not preclude this. "Harm" (al-sharr) means poverty, sickness and the like, and the definite article (al) is for the category, i.e., "when the category of harm touches him."

﴿Jaza'an (distressed)﴾, i.e., exceedingly anxious, excessive in distress.

Al-Raghib said: *al-jaza'* is more intense than *al-huzn* (grief), since *al-huzn* is general, whereas *al-jaza'* is a grief that turns a person away from what he is aiming at and cuts him off from it. Its root meaning is cutting a rope in half; one says *jaza'uhu* and *faniaja'a* (he cut it and it was cut). Because of the notion of severance in it, a valley's end is called *jaza' al-wadi* (the valley's cut-off point). Severance also refers to a change of color, and so colored beads are called *jaza'*. From this is borrowed the expression *lahm mujazza'* (meat of two colors), since it has two hues. It is also said of a date (busrah) when ripening has reached half of it that it is *mujazza'ah* (half-ripened).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 21:

﴿When evil touches him,﴾ that is, wealth and affluence, or health, ﴿he is excessively stingy﴾, exaggerating in withholding and holding back. (The first "idha") is an adverbial clause (zarf) governing "jaz'an" (anxious), and the second is an adverbial clause governing "manu'an" (stingy). These two descriptions, according to what some eminent scholars have chosen, are explanatory qualifiers (sifatan kashifatan) for "halu'an" (greedy), which falls in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), as is most fitting in light of what you have heard from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

Others said: "The three descriptions are circumstantial clauses (ahwal). It is said they are prospective (muqaddarah) if what is meant is that the human being is characterized by these traits in actuality, since at the time of creation he was not like that; rather, this came to him after the completion of his intellect and his entry into moral obligation (taklif). And they are actual (muhaqqaqah) if what is meant is that he is characterized by the source (mabda') of these matters, from the innate natural dispositions and the universal temperaments in which these traits are included potentially. According to the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq), there is no impediment to God, exalted is He, creating man and imprinting on him, glorified is He, that disposition." Regarding whether these traits can be removed afterward, there is disagreement. It is said that they can be removed by treatment, and otherwise there would be no benefit in forbidding them and prohibiting them; and they are not among the necessary properties of the quiddity (mahiyyah), so God, exalted is He, who created them, removes them. It is also said: they cannot be removed; rather, they are concealed, and a person is prevented from their outward effects, as it has been said:

"The natural disposition in a human being does not change."

This disagreement applies to all natural matters. Some said: the matters that follow from the basic temperament do not change, while those that follow from an accident of it may change.

Al-Zamakhshari held that there is a metaphor (isti'arah) in the speech. He said: the meaning is that man, because of his preference for anxiety and withholding, and their firm establishment and entrenchment in him, is as if he were innately disposed to them, naturally inclined, and as if it were an innate and necessary matter, not a matter of choice, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya: 37], because in the womb and the cradle he had no anxiety. Also, it is a reproach, and God, exalted is He, does not reproach His own act, glorified is He. The evidence for this is the exception of the believers who struggled against their souls, compelled them toward hardships, and divested them of desires, until they were neither anxious nor withholding.

This has been objected to: in the cradle he is indeed most anxious and eager (ahla' wa ahla'), so he hastens to the breast and is keen on nursing; if pain touches him he becomes anxious and weeps; if he grasps something and is crowded over it, he withholds it with whatever power he has, with agitation and crying. In the womb, his state is not known. Also, the name applies to him only after birth, so what comes after it is the relevant consideration. And the reproach is with respect to the servant's own conduct, as has been established in its proper place. As for the exception, it is either disjunctive (munqati'), because when He, glorified is He, described those who turned away and withdrew, attributing it to their anxiety and dread, He said, exalted is He: ﴿But those who pray﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 35] in contrast to them, ﴿they are in gardens﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 35], then He returned to the earlier subject and said ﴿So what is wrong with those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 36], with the particle "fa" indicating specification after generalization, and they returned to the beginning, because they are among the mockers whose mention of questioning opened the surah. Or it is connected (muttasil), on the basis that their creation did not continue in dread; for the first, being a causal explanation, meant a creation continuously characterized by dread and anxiety, ﴿except those who pray﴾, for their creation did not continue in that way. So it is not objected that if the dread in the cradle were intended, the exception of those who pray would not be valid, since they are like others in childhood. End. This exception is what is contained in His saying, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verses 22–23:

﴿Except those who pray﴾, etc. He (glorified is He) has described them with what indicates the perfection of their freedom from anxiety (al-hala')—arising from being absorbed in obedience to the Real (Mighty and Majestic), from compassion toward creation, from belief in recompense, from fear of punishment, from breaking desire, and from preferring the Hereafter over the present life. So the Mighty and Majestic Speaker said: ﴿who are constant in their prayer﴾, meaning: those who are persistent in performing it, who do not neglect it, and who are not distracted from it by any of the distractions. In this is an indication of the virtue of persistence in worship.

Ibn Hibban narrated from Abu Salamah, who said: "A'ishah told me, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Take of the deeds what you are able to do, for Allah does not tire until you tire.' She said: The most beloved of deeds to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was that which was done constantly, even if it was little. And when he prayed a prayer, he would persist in it."

Abu Salamah recited ﴿who are constant in their prayer﴾. Ahmad narrated in his Musnad from her that she said: "His (ﷺ) deed was constant (diymah)." Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said: that is, he did no act of goodness except that he had become accustomed to it and would perform it whenever its time came. It has been objected that the verb form (al-fi'lah) denotes the state in which the person persists, and then making the very state [of the person] to be the act involves an exaggeration that is not hidden, and an indication that it was a settled disposition (malakah) for him, upon him be prayer and peace. It was also said that ﴿constant﴾ means they do not turn their attention during it (i.e., in the prayer), and from this comes "stagnant water" (al-ma' al-da'im). This was narrated from Imran ibn Husayn, and likewise from Uqbah ibn Amir. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Khayr that Uqbah said to them: "Who are those who are constant in their prayer?" They said: "Those who never cease praying." He said: "No, rather those who, when they pray, do not turn left or right." Al-Zajjaj also took this view. Thus the verse indicates the reprehensibility of turning one's attention during prayer, and the reports have spoken to this; some scholars cited it as evidence that it is a major sin, and its verification is in al-Zawajir.

From Ibn Mas'ud and Masruq: that its constancy is performing it at its appointed times. This, as you see, is [weak]; perhaps the avoidance of turning and performing it on time is included in what follows of guarding it, God willing. By "prayer" is meant, according to what Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibrahim al-Taymi, the obligatory prayer. And from Imam Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, that what is meant is the supererogatory prayer.

It was also said: what they were commanded with of it, in general. Al-Hasan recited "salawatihim" (their prayers) in the plural.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verses 24–25:

﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾ i.e., a specific portion which they make binding upon themselves, seeking nearness to Allah the Exalted and out of compassion for the people. Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And those who affirm the Day of Judgment﴾.

The intended meaning is affirming it through deeds, whereby they exert themselves in bodily acts of worship, hoping for the reward of the Hereafter, because mere inward assent (al-taṣdīq al-qalbī) is shared by all Muslims, and none among them is distinguished by it. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 27:

﴿And those who are fearful of the punishment of their Lord﴾ (who are apprehensive for themselves), despite the righteous deeds they have, considering them few (istiqsar) and magnifying His presence (istiz'am li-janabihi), Mighty and Majestic is He, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they are returning to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 29–32:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 34:

﴿And those who are, over their prayer, guarding (it)﴾ — i.e., they observe its conditions (shara'it) and complete its obligatory acts (fara'id), its sunan (the emphasized Sunnah acts) and its recommended acts (mustahabbat). This is by way of the metaphor of "guarding" (hifz) from being lost, applied to completion and perfecting. This is other than "constancy" (dawam), for constancy refers to the prayers themselves, whereas this refers to their states. Therefore it does not repeat what preceded in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾. It seems that, since what is observed in completing and perfecting the prayer varies according to times, the present tense indicating renewal was used; so it is said. And it is said that the use of it together with the fronting of "hum" (they) is for greater emphasis on this ruling, since the matter of piety in such a case is stronger than in the case of "hum muhafizun" (they are guarders). This was considered here and not in the opening, because the observance mentioned is often neglected. In opening the attributes with what relates to the prayer and closing with it there is an indication of its nobility and the loftiness of its rank, for it is the ascent (mi'raj) of the believers and the intimate conversation (munajah) with the Lord of the worlds, and for this reason it was made the delight of the eye of the master of the messengers (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions, all of them. The repetition of the relative pronouns (al-ladhina) is to treat the difference of attributes as the difference of essences, signalling that each one of the mentioned attributes is a distinguished quality in its own right, having a great status, entailing numerous rulings, deserving to be assigned a separate, independent subject, and that none of them should be made a complement of another.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 35:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the people described by the qualities mentioned earlier. The sense of distance in it is due to the distance of those referred to, either in rank (al-fadl) or in mention, with regard to the source (mabda') of the qualities mentioned. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿in gardens﴾, meaning: they are settled in gardens whose measure cannot be estimated and whose reality cannot be grasped. His, may He be exalted, words ﴿honoured﴾ are another predicate, or it is the predicate itself, with "in gardens" (fi jannat) being related to it, placed before it for emphasis (li'tima'm) while observing the rhyme (fawasil). Or it is related to an implied verb which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the predicate, meaning: honoured, existing in gardens.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verses 36–37:**

﴿So what is the matter with those who disbelieve, rushing towards you from before you﴾, that is, in the direction that faces you. ﴿Hastening (muhti'in)﴾, hurrying towards you, stretching out their necks toward you, turning their eyes fixedly upon you, in order to catch [something] they make a mockery of. ﴿Scattered (ʿizin) to the right and to the left﴾, groups in dispersed formation, as Abu ʿUbayda said, and they cited the verse of ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras:

*So they came hurrying to him, until they were around his pulpit in groups (ʿizīn).*

Some scholars specified that each group (ʿizah) consists of about three or four persons. It is the plural of ʿizah, and its origin is ʿizwah, from ʿizz (strength/honour), because each faction takes pride in and claims affiliation to something other than what the other faction claims. Its last radical is thus a waw. It has also been said that its last radical is a hāʾ, and the original is ʿizhah, and it was pluralised with the waw and nūn as sanah and its sisters were. The ʿayn may be vowelled with a kasra or a ḍamma in the plural. They said: ʿizy on the pattern fiʿl, and they did not say ʿizāt. ʿIzīn is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, or of the pronoun in ﴿hastening﴾, by interlacing (tadākhul). ﴿To the right﴾ is either connected to it, since it carries the sense of "scattering", or to "hastening", meaning hastening from both directions, or it is itself a state, meaning existing as scattered to the right.

It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, used to pray near the Kaʿba and recite the Qurʾan, and the polytheists would gather around him in circles and groups, listening and mocking his words, peace be upon him, and saying: "If these people enter Paradise as Muhammad (ﷺ) says, then we will enter it before them." So this was revealed.

In some reports there is an indication that it is preferable that the believers do not sit in scattered groups, because it is a custom of the Jahiliyya.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 39:**

﴿Nay﴾, a rebuke to them for that vain greed, ﴿Indeed, We created them from what they know﴾.

It has been said that this is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of the rebuke, and the meaning is: "We created them for the sake of what they know," which is the perfecting of the soul through faith and obedience. Whoever does not perfect his soul in this way is far from attaining the station of the perfected. So how can they hope to enter Paradise while they are devoted to disbelief, wickedness, and denial of the Resurrection? Their knowledge of this is based on their hearing it from the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said that "min" (from) is the "min" of origin (ibtida'iyya), and the meaning is that they were created from a foul drop (nutfa qadhira) that does not suit the world of holiness (alam al-qudus). So when it is not perfected by faith and obedience, and is not adorned with the characteristics of the angels, peace be upon them, it is not prepared to enter it. Both opinions, as you see, are weak.

The Mufti of the Rumi lands (the Ottoman lands) said: the closer view is that this is a new independent sentence (kalaman musta'nafan), introduced as a preface to what follows of the explanation of His, exalted and majestic is He, power to destroy them for their disbelief in the Resurrection and the Recompense, their mockery of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of what was revealed to him of the Revelation, upon him be blessings and peace, and their claim, in mockery, that they would enter Paradise, ﴿and bring in others in their place﴾. For His power, glorified is He, over what they know of the first creation is a clear proof of His power, exalted and majestic is He, over that. This is what the eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasiha) in His, exalted is He, saying reveals (ma yufsihu anhu al-fa' al-fasiha fi qawlihi ta'ala).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verses 40–41:

﴿So I swear not by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ meaning: since the matter is as We have mentioned, that their creation is from what they know, namely the vile drop (nutfah), ﴿So I swear not by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾. ﴿Indeed, We are able﴾ ﴿to replace them with better than them﴾, meaning: We could destroy them entirely, as their crimes require, and bring in place of them other creatures who are not of their description. ﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾, meaning: not overcome, if We wished that. But Our will, which is based on profound wisdoms, required the delay of their punishments. In this there is a kind of remoteness, and perhaps the closer reading is that it carries the sense of causation (ta'lil), but in a manner that al-Alusi's source, Sahib al-Kashf (al-Taybi), established from the words of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). He said: he meant that it is a restraint from greed, justified by their denial of the Resurrection, since mention of its proof occurs only with the one who denies it. So the cause of the cause is placed in the position of the cause, for emphasis, since what was reported about them was their greed to enter Paradise.

Clearly, this contradicts the state of one who does not affirm it, so it is as if it were said: he denies the Resurrection, so ﴿how~﴾ could his greed be directed (toward Paradise)? He argued against them by their creation first, and by God's power, glorified is He, to create the like of them second. In this there is a mockery of them and an alert to the place of their contradiction, for mocking the Hour and greed for entry into Paradise are mutually contradictory. The reason it is closer is the strength of its connection with what preceded it, though in reality it is the more remote in purport. From this it is known that what has been said regarding His words, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, We are able﴾ ﴿to replace﴾, etc., that its meaning is ﴿Indeed, We are able﴾ to give Muhammad (ﷺ) those who are better than them, namely the Ansar, is not correct. In the expression about the substance of their creation as "what they know," there is what breaks the pride of the arrogant, which is not hidden.

By "the easts and the wests" is meant the hundred and eighty easts of the sun and its hundred and eighty wests, likewise; or the easts and wests of the sun and the moon, as narrated from Ikrimah; or the easts and wests of the stars in general, as has been said. Some have gone to the view that what is meant is the Lord of all creatures together. The discussion of ﴿So I do not swear﴾ has already passed. Some read "fa-la qasama" without alif, and 'Abdullah ibn Muslim, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read "al-mashriq wal-maghrib" in the singular.

Abu Bakr related from Asim that he read ﴿yukhrajuna﴾ in the passive form from the causative (ikhraj), ﴿swiftly (sira'an)﴾, meaning hastening, and it is an accusative of state (hal) from the nominative subject of ﴿yakhruju﴾. It is the plural of sari' (swift), like zarif and zirafan. ﴿As if they were rushing to a idol (nusub)﴾, which is what is set up and worshipped besides Allah, mighty and majestic is He. Many scholars count it as singular, and he (al-Alusi) recited the verse of al-A'sha:

"And the set-up idol, do not worship it, but worship Allah, your Lord, for the sake of the outcome."

Some said it is the plural of nisab, like kitab and kutub. Al-Akhfash said it is the plural of nasb, like rahn and ruhun, and al-ansab is the plural of the plural. The majority read ﴿nusbin﴾ with a fathah on the nun and sukun on the sad. It is a singular noun, and it is said to mean an idol set up for worship, or a marker set up on the road so that the traveler may be guided by it.

Abu Amr said it is a net in which game falls, and its owner hurries to it for fear the game will escape. It is also said to be whatever is set up as a sign of the king's arrival and journey. Abu Imran al-Hawfi and Mujahid read ﴿nasabin﴾ with fathah on both the nun and the sad, a form (fa'al) in the sense of maf'ul (object). Al-Hasan and Qatadah read ﴿nusbin﴾ with dammah on the nun and sukun on the sad, either as a lightened form of nusub with two dammahs, or as the plural of nasab with two fathahs, like walad and wulud.

﴿Yuifidun﴾ means they hasten. The root of iifad, as al-Raghib said, is that the one who has the wafadah (a quiver), which is the kinanah, runs and it rattles upon him, then it was used for hastening. It is also said that it is a general term for setting out.

It is related from al-Dahhak, and most scholars hold the first meaning, that the intended sense is that they come out hastening towards the caller, each one overtaking the other. Hastening in travel towards falsely worshipped objects was a habit of the polytheists. We have seen many of their counterparts who worship the tombs of the imams and the like, may Allah be pleased with them, doing the same. Likewise, it is the habit of one who has lost the way to hasten towards its markers, and the habit of soldiers to hasten towards the king's encampment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 70, verse 44:

﴿Their eyes downcast﴾ because of the greatness of what they have come to realize; the eyes are described as downcast, although it is a description of the whole person, because of the extreme manifestation of its effects upon them. ﴿Humiliation will cover them﴾ (taghshahum), ﴿severe humiliation﴾ (shadidah). ﴿That﴾ (dhalika), referring to what was mentioned of the terrifying conditions that will befall them in it, ﴿is the Day which they were promised﴾, i.e., in the worldly life.

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is the subject (mubtada'), "al-yawm" is the predicate (khabar), the relative pronoun is its qualifier (sifah), and the clause following it is its relative clause (silah). The returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "yuw'adunahu" (they were promised it). ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Khilad, on the authority of Dawud ibn Salim, on the authority of Ya'qub, and al-Hasan ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, on the authority of al-Tammar, read "«dhillati»" without tanwin, in the genitive construction with "dhalika al-yawm" (that day) in the genitive case. This is noted.

Know that some of the Sufis in this age have mentioned, concerning this Day, of which God Most High informed that its measure is fifty thousand years, that the levels (al-maratib) are four: the realm of the Kingdom (al-mulk), the Malakut, the Jabarut, and the Lahut; and each higher level encompasses the lower, and the one above it is ten degrees higher, because it is the completion of the level, since God created things from ten handfuls (qabadat), meaning from the secret of the ten levels of the nine spheres and the elements in each world according to its measure. For this reason the levels of numbers are arranged upon the four, and the thousand is the final level and the furthest goal.

And since the relation to the Lord, i.e., to the direction of the Truth, is the ultimate end relative to all else ("To your Lord is the final end" [al-Najm: 42]), the single day attributed to Him was a thousand years; for this reason the lordly day is a thousand years, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. Thus, when existence ascends and wisdom requires the manifestation of the other creation and the emergence of the effects of the Greatest Name at the station of divinity, in the rank of the All-Comprehensive, existence, the cosmoses and the beings come forth in one assembly according to their levels in the entities. So the secret of the letter nun appeared from the word ﴿Be﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117 and elsewhere], for the manifestation of "fa-yakun" (and it is). Thus the fifty appeared in the return, as it descended at the beginning, and this is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿As He originated you, so you will return﴾ [al-A'raf: 29]. So the single day, at the manifestation of the Greatest Name in the all-comprehensive direction, was fifty thousand years; the thousand is for the ascent of the one, and since the levels are fifty, it was fifty thousand, and the fifty are the details of the manifestation of the name of the Lord at the manifestation of the name of Allah in the world of command, which is the first level of detail in His saying, Most High, ﴿Be﴾. The first manifestation of detail was fifty, because the unity manifest in the point, the alif, the letters, the complete word, and the indication which is the completion of the five, was only in the ten worlds of the levels of determinations; or because the four natures, together with the attainment of mixture through the appearance of a fifth nature, by which the five are complete, were only in ten worlds, which he counts; so the total was fifty. The ten worlds are: the world of possibility, the world of the heart (fu'ad), the world of the qalb, the world of the intellect, the world of the spirit, the world of the soul, the world of nature, the world of matter, the world of image, and the world of bodies.

The fifty, in the face of the Lord and the direction of the Truth, in the first world, which is the last, will be fifty thousand years. End. If you understand from it a correct meaning, which sound minds accept and transmitted texts do not reject, then so be it; otherwise, praise God Most High for well-being, and ask Him, Mighty and Majestic, for success in reaching the landmarks of verification. Al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, also has a discourse on this station, so whoever wishes it should follow his books, and let him ask God Most High for openings, for He, glory be to Him, is the Giver of gifts.
